newsitem.title: RUSSIA: AGROKHLEB - Russia's 96/97 wheat imports to fall.
newsitem.headline: AGROKHLEB - Russia's 96/97 wheat imports to fall.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from SovEcon Ltd, an independent research organisation specialising in agricultural production and trade in the former Soviet Union.
SOVECON SEES RUSSIA'S 96/97 WHEAT IMPORTS DOWN YEAR-ON-YEAR
MOSCOW, March 24 - SovEcon expects Russia's total wheat imports in 1996/97 to decline to about 2 million tonnes from 3.2 million tonnes in 1995/96.
Kazakhstan remains the major supplier in 1996/97, accounting for around 70 percent of Russia's total wheat imports.
Over July 1996-February 1997, wheat imports in most Russian regions declined on year-ago levels, especially in Western and Eastern Siberia, the Urals and the Volga river regions.
The decline reflects better wheat output in 1996 and, particularly, financial constraints that have limited the effective demand of potential buyers.
However, the decline in wheat imports by the Central and Northwest regions is relatively smaller than in other areas.
The decline is caused by tight milling wheat stocks in the Northern Caucasus, which is the major supplier to consuming regions in the European part of Russia.
As a result, the Central and Northwest regions accounted for nearly a half of Russia's total wheat imports in July 1996-February 1997, compared to 38.4 percent over the same period in 1995/96.
The Far East's share in total imports has also increased, while Western Siberia's has declined.
Despite some increase in wheat production and reduced demand, the supply situation is quite tight.
In February 1997, wheat imports increased to 162,000 tonnes, compared to 79,000 tonnes in January.
Imported wheat deliveries to Moscow rose (74,500 tonnes in February against 20,800 tonnes in January). Deliveries to Yaroslav Oblast (Central Region) increased to 14,600 tonnes from 600.
In February, most industrial areas (Leningrad, Moscow, Nizhnegorod, Samara, Chelyabinsk) also increased their imports.
Assuming a normal rate of consumption, wheat-consuming areas, particularly in the European part of Russia, are likely to continue to increase their wheat imports this spring.
